Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 1:

(p-518) Surat "al-Qalam" (The Pen)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Nun.﴾ The apparent meaning is that by it is intended this letter of the letters of the alphabet (al-mu'jam). As for the saying of al-Hasan, "It is the inkwell (al-dawah)," and the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, "It is the fish upon which the earth rests, and its name is Yahmut," these are problematic, because it must have a case-ending (i'rab), whether it is a common noun (ism jins) or a proper name (ism 'alam). Therefore the sukun (vowellessness) is evidence that it is one of the letters of spelling out (huruf al-tahajji).

﴿By the pen,﴾ that is: that with which the Preserved Tablet was written, or "the pen of the angels," or that with which people write. He swore by it because of what it contains of benefits and advantages which description cannot encompass.

﴿And what they inscribe,﴾ that is: what the recording angels (al-hafazah) inscribe, or what is written with it of good by whoever writes. "Ma" is either a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah).

And the answer of the oath:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 2:

﴿You are not, by the grace of your Lord, a madman.﴾ That is: by His bestowing on you prophethood and other things. So "anta" (you) is the subject (ism) of "ma" (not), and its predicate (khabar) is ﴿a madman﴾ (bi-majnun). "Bi-ni'mati Rabbika" (by the grace of your Lord) is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) between the subject and the predicate. The "ba'" (bi) in "bi-ni'mati Rabbika" is related to an omitted element, and its position (mahall) is the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal); the governing element within it is "bi-majnun." Its implied sense is: "You are not a madman, having been blessed with that."

The "ba'" does not prevent "majnun" from governing what precedes it, because it is an added (za'idah) particle used to emphasize the negation. This is the answer to their saying: (p-519) ﴿And they say: O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are surely a madman﴾ [al-Hijr: 6].

﴿And indeed, for you﴾, in return for bearing that and being patient with it,

﴿is a reward﴾, that is, a recompense,

﴿never-ending﴾, that is, never cut off; or never-ending in the sense that it is not bestowed upon you with obligation (lit. "not something reckoned as a favour upon you because of it").

﴿And indeed you are of a great moral character﴾. It was said: it is what Allah (Exalted) commanded him in His saying: ﴿Hold to forgiveness, enjoin what is right, and turn away from the ignorant﴾ [al-A'raf: 199]. ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "His character was the Qur'an," meaning: what is in it of noble character traits. He was described as having a great character because he gave generously of both worlds and relied upon the Creator of both.
Verse 5 (al-Qalam): ﴿So you will see, and they will see﴾. That is, soon you will see and they will see. This is a promise to him, and a warning to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 6:

﴿Which of you is the afflicted﴾, al-majnun (the madman), because "futina" means he was tested with madness (muhina bil-junun). The bāʾ (in bi-ayyikum) is superfluous (mazīdah). Or "al-maftun" is a verbal noun (maṣdar), like "al-maʿqul", meaning: which of you is the madness. Al-Zajjaj said: the bāʾ has the meaning of "fī" (in), as you say "kuntu bi-baladi kadha", meaning "fī baladi kadha" (I was in such-and-such a city). Its estimated form is: "in which of you is the afflicted", meaning: in which of the two groups among you is the madman, the group of Islam or the group of disbelief.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 7:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who has strayed from His way﴾. That is: He is most knowing of the madmen (majanin) in reality, and they are those who have strayed from His way.

﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾. That is: He is most knowing of the people of intellect ('uqala'), and they are those who are guided.

"So do not obey the deniers." This is an incitement to firmness in their opposition (mu'asat), for they wished that he would worship God for a period and their gods for a period, and that they would ward off from him their harms (ghawa'il).

﴿They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾. "Would compromise" means: be lenient toward them, so that they would be lenient toward you. The verb ﴿فَيُدْهِنُونَ﴾ (fa-yudhinun, "so they would compromise") is not put in the subjunctive by an implied "an" (أنْ), even though it answers the wish (جَوابُ التَمَنِّي, jawab al-tamanni, "the response to the expressed wish"). The reason is that he (the grammarian) moved it to another construction, namely that it was made the predicate (خَبَرَ, khabar) of an omitted subject (مُبْتَدَأ, mubtada', "subject of a nominal sentence"), meaning: "fa-hum yudhinun" (so they are compromising), that is: "fa-hum al-an yudhinun, due to their greed for your compromise" (so they are now compromising, out of their eagerness for you to compromise).

(p-520) ﴿And do not obey every constant swearer﴾, one who swears often, whether in truth or falsehood. And this is sufficient as a deterrent for one who is accustomed to swearing.

﴿Contemptible﴾: lowly in opinion and discernment, from "al-mahana" (contemptibility), which means scantiness and baseness. Or (he is) a liar, because he is contemptible in the eyes of people.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 11:

﴿Hammaz﴾ (one who backbites, slanders openly), ʿayyab (one who finds fault), ṭaʿʿan (one who defames), mughtab (one who backbites in absence),

﴿mashshaʾ bi-namim﴾ (one who goes about spreading tale-bearing), naqqal lil-hadith (one who carries speech) min qawm ila qawm (from one people to another), ʿala wajh al-saʿaya wal-ifsad baynahum (with the intent of stirring up mischief and corruption among them). And "al-namim" and "al-namimah" mean: tale-bearing (al-saʿaya).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 12:

﴿Forbidder of the good﴾, stingy. "Al-khayr" (the good): wealth; or, he forbids his people from the good, which is Islam. The intended person is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, according to the majority (al-Jumhur). He used to say to his ten sons: "Whoever among you embraces Islam, I will withhold my bounty (rifd) from him."

﴿Transgressor﴾, one who exceeds his limit in wrongdoing.

﴿Sinful﴾, one who commits many sins.

﴿Utull﴾ (ʿutull): harsh, coarse and hard-hearted.

﴿After that﴾: after all of the defects that were enumerated for him.

﴿Zanim﴾ (zanīm): an illegitimate, adopted-in-name person (duʿiyy). Al-Walid was an illegitimate claimant among Quraysh; he was not of their stock (sinkh). His father claimed him eighteen years after his birth. It is also said that his mother had committed adultery, and he was not recognized until this verse was revealed. "When the seed is corrupt, the one who grows from it is corrupt." It is narrated that he entered upon his mother and said: "Muhammad (ﷺ) described me with ten qualities; I have found nine of them in myself. As for the zanim, I have no knowledge of it. So if you tell me its truth, well and good; otherwise I will strike your neck." She said: "Your father was impotent (ʿinnīn), and I feared that he would die and his wealth would pass to someone other than his son, so I invited a shepherd to myself, and you are from that shepherd."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 14:

﴿Because he has wealth and sons.﴾ It is related (mut'alliq) to his saying: "and do not obey", meaning: do not obey him, despite these blemishes, because "he has wealth", that is, because of his affluence and his share of this world. It is also permissible for it to be related to what follows it, meaning: because "he has wealth and sons, he denied Our signs", which is indicated by:

﴿When Our verses are recited to him﴾, i.e., the Qur'an,

﴿he says, "Tales of the ancients."﴾ The word "قال" (qāla, "he said") does not govern the conditional clause here, because what follows the conditional particle (sharṭ) cannot govern what precedes it. "أأنْ" (ʾan, with the hamza read as a question): Ḥamza and Abū Bakr read it. That is, "ألِأنْ كانَ ذا مالٍ كَذَبَ" ("Is it because he possessed wealth that he lied?"). "آنْ" (ān): al-Shāmī, Yazīd, Yaʿqūb and Sahl read it. They said: When al-Walīd (ra) disparaged the Prophet (ﷺ) as a liar with one name, which is "the madman," (p-521) Allah (Exalted) named him truthful with ten names. If it was part of His justice that He repays the evildoer against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with ten, it was part of His grace that whoever sends one blessing upon him, He sends upon him ten in return.

﴿سَنَسِمُهُ﴾, that is, We will brand him,

﴿عَلَى الخُرْطُومِ﴾, on his snout, meaning on his nose, as a humiliation for him and a mark by which he would be known. The nose is singled out for mention because branding on it is more disfiguring. It is also said that his snout was struck with a sword on the day of Badr, and the scar remained on his snout.

﴿Indeed, We tested them﴾: We tested the people of Makkah with drought and hunger, to the point that they ate carrion and bones, through the supplication of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he said: "O Allah, make Your foot fall heavily upon Mudar, and make its years like the years of Yusuf."

﴿As We tested the companions of the garden﴾: They were a people from among the People of Prayer (ahl al-salah). Their father had this garden in a village called Dharwan, which was two farsakhs (a unit of distance) from San'a'. He would take from it the provision for a year and give the remainder in charity to the poor. When he died, his sons said: "If we do what our father used to do, the matter will be hard for us, and we are people with dependants." So they swore that they would harvest it at dawn, in the darkness, secretly from the needy, and they did not make an exception (istithna', a conditional exception such as "if God wills") in their oath. So God burned their garden. Al-Hasan said: "They were disbelievers." But the majority hold the first view.

﴿When they swore﴾: they took an oath,

﴿that they would surely harvest it﴾: they would surely cut its fruit,

﴿at dawn﴾: entering into the morning, before the poor dispersed. It is a circumstantial clause (hal, a circumstantial accusative) from the subject of "لَيَصْرِمُنَّها", which is to say from the subject of the verb that precedes it.

﴿And they did not make exception⦆, meaning they did not say, "If God wills." It is called "exception" (istithna'), even though it is grammatically in the form of a conditional (shart), because it performs the function of an exception (istithna'), in that the meaning of your saying, "I will certainly go out, if God wills," and "I will not go out except that God wills," is one and the same.

﴿Then a visitation from your Lord swept over it﴾: a calamity descended upon it. It was said: God (Exalted is He) sent down upon it a fire, and it burned it.

﴿while they were sleeping﴾, i.e., during the state of their sleep.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 20:

﴿So it became﴾: that is, the garden became

﴿like the ṣarīm (a dark, stripped night)﴾: like the pitch-dark night. That is, it was burned and turned black. Or, "like the dawn," that is, (p-522) it became white land without any trees. It was also said: "like the maṣrūmah (harvested or cut off)," that is, as if it had been harvested because its fruit had been destroyed.
﴿So they called out to one another at dawn﴾, [that is,] some of them called to others at the morning time.

﴿That go out early﴾, i.e., go out at dawn,

﴿to your field﴾. He did not say "إلى حرثكم" (ilā ḥarthikum, "to your field"), because going out to it in order to cut its produce was a going out upon it, or the verb ghudūw (going out, setting out) was used with the meaning of iqbāl (turning towards, applying oneself), i.e., "so apply yourselves to your field, going out early."

﴿if you are going to harvest﴾, meaning, intending to cut its produce.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 23:**

﴿So they set off﴾: they went away.

﴿while they were speaking in low voices to one another﴾: they were confiding secretly among themselves, so that the poor would not hear.

ۣ"That they should not let any needy person enter it" — here is the translation:

﴿That no poor man shall enter it today upon you﴾ — that is, the Garden. The "an" (أنْ) is explanatory (mufassirah). It is also read with the particle dropped, with the verb of saying understood (bi-idmar al-qawl), meaning: they whisper to one another, saying: "No poor man shall enter it today upon you."

The prohibition against the entry of the poor is a prohibition against enabling them, meaning: do not allow him to enter.

"And they went forth early, [determined] upon prevention" — "upon intense resolve to withhold" (ʿalā jidd fī al-manʿ),

"capable [in their own estimation]" — "capable, in their own view, of withholding [the fruit]." So Naṭṭawayh (Nafṭawayh) reported, or: "al-ḥard" means intention and haste, i.e. they went forth to their garden swiftly, intending [it], "capable in their own estimation of harvesting it and cutting off its benefit from the poor." Or it is a proper name for the garden: they went forth to that garden, capable of harvesting it in their own estimation.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 26:

﴿When they saw it﴾, that is, their garden, burnt black,

﴿they said﴾, at the very moment of their arrival,

﴿"Indeed, we have gone astray"﴾, that is: we have lost our garden, and this is not it, because of what they saw of its destruction. Then, when they considered carefully and recognized that it was indeed it, they said:

Qur'anic verse: ﴿Nay, we are deprived.﴾ "We have been deprived of its good, because of our crime against ourselves."

Note on the passage: the Arabic is short, so the translation follows it closely.

﴿He who was most moderate among them said﴾, the most just of them and the best of them.

﴿Did I not tell you, "Why do you not glorify [God]?"﴾ Why do you not make the exception (istithna', saying "if God wills")? The istithna' is the tasbih (glorifying God, saying "Glory be to God"), because they meet in the meaning of exalting God. The istithna' is entrusting the matter to Him, and the tasbih is declaring Him free of imperfection (tanzih). Each of the entrusting (tafwid) and the declaring-free (tanzih) is an exalting (ta'zim).

Or: "Why do you not remember God and repent to Him for the wickedness of your intention?" When they resolved upon that, their most moderate one said to them: "Remember God and His retribution against the criminals, and repent of this wicked resolve (p-523)." But they disobeyed him, so he rebuked them, and for this [reason]

"They said, 'Glory be to our Lord! Indeed we were wrongdoers.'" Then, after the destruction of their orchard, they spoke with what had called them to speak earlier, acknowledged against themselves the wrong of withholding what is good and of abandoning the exception (in saying "if God wills"), and declared Him far above being a wrongdoer.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 30:

﴿So they turned to one another, blaming each other.﴾ He blames one another for what they had done, namely fleeing from the poor (al-masakin), and each one of them throws the blame onto the other. Then they all admitted that they had exceeded the limit, by his saying:

They said, "O woe to us! Indeed we were transgressors," (بِمَنعِ حَقِّ الفُقَراءِ، وتَرْكِ الِاسْتِثْناءِ) — by withholding the right of the poor, and by neglecting to say "if God wills" (al-istithna').

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 32:

﴿Perhaps our Lord will give us in exchange﴾, and with the doubled letter (tashdid) [it is read] by Madani and Abu 'Amr,

﴿something better than it﴾, than this garden,

﴿Indeed, to our Lord we turn with desire﴾, seeking good from Him, returning to His pardon. From Mujahid: "They repented, so they were given in exchange something better than it." And from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him: "It has reached me that they sincerely turned back, so He gave them in its place a garden called (al-Hayawan), in which there are grapes, of which a mule could carry a single cluster."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 33:

﴿Such is the punishment﴾, i.e., like that punishment which We have mentioned, the punishment of this world, for whoever follows their path,

﴿and the punishment of the Hereafter is greater﴾, greater than it,

﴿if only they knew﴾, they would not have done what leads to this punishment. Then he mentioned what is with Him for the believers, saying:

Indeed, for those who are mindful (of God), (﴿إنَّ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ﴾), (who guard themselves) against shirk (associating partners with God),

﴿عِنْدَ رَبِّهِمْ﴾ means: in the Hereafter,

﴿جَنّاتِ النَعِيمِ﴾ "gardens of bliss," gardens in which there is nothing but pure enjoyment, unlike the gardens of this world.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 35:

﴿Shall We then treat the Muslims like the criminals?﴾ It is a rhetorical question of denunciation (istifham inkar) directed at their saying: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we will be given in the Hereafter better than what he and those with him are given, just as in this world." So it was said to them: "Do We deviate in judgement, so that We treat the Muslims like the disbelievers?!" Then it was said to them, by way of iltifat (a shift from address to third-person reference), [...]

﴿What is the matter with you? How do you judge?﴾ This crooked judgment, namely the equating of the obedient with the disobedient, as if the matter of recompense were entrusted to you, so that you could judge concerning it however you wish.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 37:

﴿Or do you have a Book﴾, from the heaven,

﴿in which you study﴾, you read in that Book.

Verse 68:38: ﴿Indeed, for you therein is that which you choose.﴾ That is: what you choose and desire is yours. The original would be "you study that for you is what you choose," with "that" (anna) vowelled with a fatha, because it is the object of studying, since the act of studying falls upon it. It is written with a kasra only because the lam has come (in the predicate). It is also permissible that it be a quotation of what is studied, as it is, like His saying: ﴿And We left for him among the later generations﴾ [al-Saffat: 78] ﴿Peace be upon Noah﴾ [al-Saffat: 79]. And "takhayyara al-shay'" and "ikhtarahu" mean: he took its best part.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 39:

﴿Or do you have oaths binding upon Us, confirmed by oaths,﴾ covenants strongly affirmed with oaths.

﴿Extending⁠﴾ is an adjective of "oaths" (aymān), and ﴿until the Day of Resurrection﴾ is connected to "extending" (bāligha), meaning that they reach that day and end at it, complete, with no oath among them having been invalidated, until what is sworn to is fulfilled from the judgment; or it is connected to what is implied in the adverbial phrase, meaning: "They are yours upon Us until the Day of Resurrection, and you will not be released from their obligation except on that day, when We make you judges and give you what you judge."

﴿Indeed, for you is what you judge⁠﴾ — for yourselves — and this is the answer of the oath, because the meaning of "Or do you have oaths binding upon Us" is: "Or have We sworn to you with emphatic oaths, extremely strong in their affirmation?!"

Ask them: which of the polytheists

(Ask them) which of them stands surety for that ruling (al-hukm).

Wait, I need to be careful and produce a faithful translation. Here it is:

﴿Ask them﴾, that is, the polytheists (al-mushrikin),

﴿which of them will vouch for that﴾, the ruling (al-hukm),

﴿is a guarantor (za'im)﴾, one who stands surety that this will be so.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 41:

﴿Or do they have associates?﴾ That is, people who share with them in this claim and follow their path in it.

﴿Then let them bring their associates, if they are truthful﴾ in their claim. This means that no one grants them this, nor supports them in it, just as they have no book in which it is spoken, nor any covenant from God concerning it, nor any guarantor (za'im) who would vouch for them from God regarding this.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 68, verse 42:

﴿On the Day the shin will be laid bare﴾. The verb governing the temporal clause (*nāṣib al-ẓarf*) is either the implied "فَلْيَأْتُوا" (*falya'tū*, "let them come") or the implied "اُذْكُرْ" (*udhkur*, "remember"). The majority of scholars hold that "uncovering the shin" is a metaphor for the intensity of the matter and the severity of the calamity. The meaning of "on the Day the shin is laid bare" is: on the Day the matter becomes intense and grave. There is no uncovering there, and no shin, but it is used as a figure of speech for severity, because when people are afflicted with a great hardship they uncover their shins. This is like saying of a miserly person with a cut hand, "his hand is shackled," though there is no hand there and no shackle; it is only a metaphor for stinginess. As for those who took it literally, this is due to the narrowness of their outlook and their lack of insight into the science of eloquence (*ʿilm al-bayān*). Had the matter been as the anthropomorphists (*al-Mushabbiha*) claim, the shin should have been made definite, since it would be a known shin to them.

﴿And they will be called﴾, that is, the disbelievers, there,

﴿to prostration﴾, not as a religious obligation, but as a rebuke for their having abandoned prostration in the world,

﴿but they will not be able﴾ to do so, because their backs will become like the horns of cattle, which do not bend when lowering or raising.

﴿Khashi'atan﴾ (humbled, abased), meaning ﴿dhalilah﴾ (humiliated), is a circumstantial clause (ḥal) referring back to the pronoun in ﴿yud'awna﴾ (they are called).

﴿Abṣāruhum﴾: that is, they are called while their eyes are humbled (khushū').

﴿Tarhaquhum dhillah﴾: humiliation overtakes them; abasement (ṣaghār) covers them.

﴿Wa-qad kānū yud'awna﴾: and they had been called, through the tongues of the Messengers,

﴿ilā al-sujūd﴾: to prostration, in the worldly life.

﴿Wa-hum sālimūn﴾: that is, while they were healthy (aṣiḥḥā'), so they would not prostrate; therefore they were prevented from prostration there (thammah).

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 44:**

﴿So leave Me﴾ (fa-dharni). It is said: "Dharni wa-iyyahu" (leave me and him), meaning: "Entrust him to Me, for I will suffice you against him."

﴿And those who deny﴾ (wa-man yukadhdhibu): it is in the accusative as a conjunction with the object (ma'tuf 'ala al-maf'ul), or as an object accompanying the verb (maf'ul ma'ahu).

﴿this discourse﴾ (bi-hadha al-hadith): that is, the Qur'an. The meaning is: entrust his affair to Me and leave between Me and him, for I am Knowing of what ought to be done to him and Able to do it. So do not occupy your heart with his affair, and rely on Me for taking vengeance upon him. This is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a threat to the deniers.

﴿We will draw them on gradually﴾ (sanastadrijuhum): We will bring them closer to the punishment step by step. It is said: "istadrajahu ila kadha" (he drew him gradually to such-and-such), meaning: he brought him down to it step by step, until he involves him in it. The drawing on of the disobedient by Allah (Exalted) is that He grants them health and blessing, and they make Allah's provision a means to increasing their acts of disobedience.

﴿from where they do not know﴾ (min haythu la ya'lamun): from the direction in which they do not perceive that it is a drawing on. It is said: whenever they renew an act of disobedience, We renew a blessing for them and make them forget its gratitude. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you see Allah (Exalted) bestowing blessings upon a servant while he persists in his disobedience, know that he is being drawn on gradually," and he recited the verse.

(p-526) ﴿And I give them respite﴾, I grant them time and delay them,

﴿Indeed, My plan is firm﴾, strong and mighty. So He called His kindness and His granting of ample means "kayd" (plan/scheme), just as He called it "istidraj" (gradual drawing-on), because it is in the form of kayd, since it was a cause of destruction. The principle is that the meaning of "al-kayd" (scheming), "al-makr" (deceit), and "al-istidraj" (gradual drawing-on) is seizing someone from a direction they feel secure from; and it is not permissible to name Allah "kaid" (one who schemes), "makir" (one who deceives), or "mustadrij" (one who draws on gradually).

Surah 68 (al-Qalam), verse 46: "Or do you ask them for a wage, so that they are burdened with debt?"

Translation of the commentary:

﴿Or do you ask them﴾, for conveying the message, ﴿a wage, so that they are burdened﴾, by a fine (gharamah), ﴿with debt﴾, and so they do not believe. The interrogative here carries the meaning of negation: that is, you do not ask for a wage for conveying the revelation, so that this would weigh heavily upon them and they would therefore refuse.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 47:

﴿Or do they have the unseen, so that they write it down?﴾ That is: the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), according to the majority (al-Jumhur).

﴿So they write it down﴾, from it they derive their judgments.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 48:

﴿So be patient with the decree of your Lord﴾, which means His delaying of them and His deferring of your victory over them, because they, even if they are given respite, are not left neglected.

﴿And do not be like the companion of the fish﴾, that is, like Yunus (peace be upon him), in his haste and his anger at his people, so that you are not afflicted with his trial. Pausing on "al-hut" (الْحُوتِ, "the fish") is correct, because "idh" (إذْ, "when") is not an adverbial of time (ẓarf) governing what precedes it, since calling upon God is an act of obedience and so is not forbidden. Rather, it is an object (maf'ūl) of a deleted verb, meaning: "Remember" (اُذْكُرْ).

﴿When he called out﴾, he called upon his Lord from within the belly of the fish, saying: "There is no god but You, glory be to You, indeed I have been among the wrongdoers."

﴿while he was suppressing his grief﴾, that is, filled with anger, from "kaẓama al-siqā'" (كَظَمَ السِقاءَ), meaning when he filled the waterskin.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 49:

﴿Had not a blessing from his Lord reached him﴾, mercy,

﴿from his Lord﴾, i.e.: had not Allah bestowed His favour upon him by answering his supplication and accepting his excuse,

﴿he would have been cast out﴾, from the belly of the fish,

﴿onto the open plain﴾, onto the open land,

﴿while he was blameworthy﴾, reproached for his lapse, but he was shown mercy, so he was cast out not blameworthy.

﴿Then his Lord chose him﴾: He selected him (iṣṭafāhu), for his supplication and his excuse (ʿudhrihi).

﴿and made him among the righteous﴾: among those who had perfected the attributes of righteousness, so that no lapse remained in him. It was said: among the prophets. It was said: among the messengers. The correct view (al-wajh) is the first, because he was a messenger and a prophet before that, due to His saying (exalted is He): ﴿And indeed Jonah was among the messengers﴾ ﴿when he fled to the laden ship﴾, and the verses that follow.

**Translation:**

﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes﴾. And reading the yā' with a fatḥa is the reading of Madanī (Nāfiʿ). "In" (إنْ) is a lightened form of the heavy (thaqīla) particle, and the lām is its marker. "Zalaqahu" and "azlaqahu" mean: he removed it from its place. That is: the disbelievers came close—out of the intensity of their gazing at you sidelong (shazaran), with eyes of enmity—to removing you from your place by their eyes, or to destroying you, because of the intensity of their rage against you. The evil eye (al-ʿayn) was among the Banū Asad, and a man among them would go hungry for three days, then something would pass by him and he would say about it: "I have not seen the like of it today," and it would perish. So some of the ʿayyānīn (those who afflict with the evil eye) were prompted to say the same about the Messenger of Allah, and he said: "I have not seen the like of him today, a man," but Allah protected him from that. In a ḥadīth: "The evil eye is real (ḥaqq), and the evil eye does indeed bring a camel into the cooking pot and a man into the grave." And from al-Ḥasan: "The ruqyah (incantation) against the evil eye is this verse."

﴿When they hear the Reminder﴾, the Qur'an,

﴿and they say﴾, out of envy at what you were given of prophethood,

﴿"Indeed he is a madman!"﴾, that Muḥammad is a madman, out of bewilderment regarding his affair, and to repel people from him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 68, verse 52:

﴿And it is not﴾, that is: the Qur'an,

﴿except a reminder﴾, an admonition,

﴿to the worlds﴾, to the jinn and mankind. That is, they called him mad because of the Qur'an; but the Qur'an is nothing except an admonition to the worlds, so how could one be called mad who has brought the like of it?

It is also said: ﴿When they heard the Reminder﴾ [al-Qalam: 51] means: his reminder (ﷺ). ﴿And it is not﴾, that is: Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿except a reminder﴾, an honour ﴿to the worlds﴾. So how can madness be ascribed to him?!
